rubric.why: The product Fe³⁺ has one more positive charge than the reactant, so the reactant is Fe²⁺.
rubric.description: Identifies the reactant ion.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for writing Fe²⁺ as the reactant.

rubric.why: The equation shows iron losing one electron to form Fe³⁺.
rubric.description: Writes the products of the oxidation equation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for showing Fe³⁺ and one electron on the product side.

modelAnswer: Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ + 1e⁻.

items.followUp: Write one difference between halogens and noble gases.

rubric.why: An alkali metal has one electron in its outermost shell.
rubric.description: States the outer-shell electron count of an alkali metal.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that an alkali metal has one valence electron.

rubric.why: An alkaline earth metal has two electrons in its outermost shell.
rubric.description: States the outer-shell electron count of an alkaline earth metal.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that an alkaline earth metal has two valence electrons.

modelAnswer: An alkali metal has one valence electron in its outermost shell.
An alkaline earth metal has two valence electrons in its outermost shell.

items.followUp: Why is hydrochloric acid a strong acid in water?

rubric.why: HF ionizes only to a limited extent in water.
rubric.description: States that HF ionizes incompletely in water.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing HF ionization as partial or incomplete.

rubric.why: Partial ionization produces relatively few hydrogen ions compared with a strong acid of the same concentration.
rubric.description: Links partial ionization to the production of relatively few hydrogen ions.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that HF produces relatively few H⁺ ions.

modelAnswer: HF is a weak acid because it ionizes only partially in water.
Consequently, it produces relatively few H⁺ ions.

items.followUp: Define an atom and describe four types of molecules classified by the number of atoms they contain.

rubric.why: A molecule is the smallest particle of a substance that can exist independently and retain its chemical properties.
rubric.description: Defines a molecule.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for defining a molecule as the smallest independently existing particle that retains the substance’s properties.

rubric.why: A monoatomic molecule contains one atom.
rubric.description: Describes a monoatomic molecule.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying a monoatomic molecule as containing one atom; an example may also be given.

rubric.why: A diatomic molecule contains two atoms.
rubric.description: Describes a diatomic molecule.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying a diatomic molecule as containing two atoms; an example may also be given.

rubric.why: A triatomic molecule contains three atoms.
rubric.description: Describes a triatomic molecule.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying a triatomic molecule as containing three atoms; an example may also be given.

rubric.why: A polyatomic molecule contains more than three atoms.
rubric.description: Describes a polyatomic molecule.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying a polyatomic molecule as containing more than three atoms; an example may also be given.

modelAnswer: A molecule is the smallest particle of a substance that can exist independently and retain its chemical properties.
A monoatomic molecule contains one atom, for example, He.
A diatomic molecule contains two atoms, for example, H₂.
A triatomic molecule contains three atoms, for example, H₂O.
A polyatomic molecule contains more than three atoms, for example, P₄.

items.followUp: Define a covalent bond and explain its formation in a hydrogen molecule.

rubric.why: An ionic bond is the electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions.
rubric.description: Defines an ionic bond.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for defining it as the electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions.

rubric.why: In sodium chloride, sodium transfers one electron to chlorine.
rubric.description: Describes electron transfer in sodium chloride.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that sodium donates one electron to chlorine.

rubric.why: The oppositely charged Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions attract to form the ionic bond.
rubric.description: Identifies the ions formed and their attraction.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for showing that Na⁺ and Cl⁻ attract to form an ionic bond.

modelAnswer: An ionic bond is the electrostatic force of attraction between oppositely charged ions.
In sodium chloride, a sodium atom transfers one electron to a chlorine atom.
Sodium becomes Na⁺ and chlorine becomes Cl⁻.
These oppositely charged ions attract each other, forming an ionic bond in NaCl.

items.followUp: Describe four differences between Thomson’s atomic model and Rutherford’s atomic model.

rubric.why: Rutherford’s model did not include fixed energy levels, whereas Bohr introduced them.
rubric.description: Contrasts the electron energy levels in the two models.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that Rutherford’s model had no fixed levels or orbits and Bohr’s model did.

rubric.why: Rutherford’s revolving electrons were expected to radiate energy; Bohr’s electrons do not radiate energy in stationary orbits.
rubric.description: Contrasts the energy behaviour of orbiting electrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for contrasting energy radiation or loss in Rutherford’s model with the stationary orbits in Bohr’s model.

rubric.why: Rutherford’s model could not explain why electrons do not spiral into the nucleus, while Bohr’s model accounts for atomic stability.
rubric.description: Contrasts the explanations of atomic stability.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that Rutherford’s model could not explain stability and Bohr’s model could.

rubric.why: Rutherford’s model could not explain the line spectrum of hydrogen, while Bohr’s model did.
rubric.description: Contrasts the models’ explanations of the line spectrum.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that Bohr explained the line spectrum that Rutherford’s model could not explain.

rubric.why: Bohr explained spectral lines through electron transitions between energy levels that emit or absorb energy.
rubric.description: Explains energy changes during electron transitions in Bohr’s model.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking electron transitions between energy levels with emission or absorption of energy.

modelAnswer: Rutherford’s model had no fixed energy levels for electrons, whereas Bohr’s model placed electrons in fixed energy levels or orbits.
Rutherford’s revolving electrons were expected to radiate energy continuously, whereas electrons in Bohr’s stationary orbits do not radiate energy.
Rutherford’s model could not explain why electrons did not spiral into the nucleus; Bohr’s model explained the stability of the atom.
Rutherford’s model could not explain the line spectrum of hydrogen, whereas Bohr’s model explained it.
In Bohr’s model, an electron transition between energy levels emits or absorbs energy; Rutherford’s model did not explain these transitions.

items.followUp: Explain how the vapour pressure of a liquid changes when its intermolecular forces become stronger and when its temperature rises.

rubric.why: The nature of the liquid affects how readily its molecules escape: stronger intermolecular forces result in lower vapour pressure.
rubric.description: Explains how the nature of a liquid affects its vapour pressure.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for relating stronger intermolecular forces to lower vapour pressure, or weaker forces to higher vapour pressure.

rubric.why: Vapour pressure increases as the temperature rises.
rubric.description: States the effect of increasing temperature.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that vapour pressure rises with temperature.

rubric.why: Heating gives molecules more kinetic energy, allowing more to escape into the vapour phase.
rubric.description: Explains why vapour pressure increases with temperature.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking the temperature increase to greater kinetic energy or more molecules escaping.

modelAnswer: The vapour pressure depends on the nature of the liquid: weaker intermolecular forces allow more molecules to escape, so vapour pressure is higher.
Liquids with stronger intermolecular forces have lower vapour pressure.
As temperature increases, the molecules gain kinetic energy and more of them escape into the vapour phase.
Therefore, vapour pressure increases as temperature rises.

items.followUp: Write down four characteristics of a suspension.

rubric.why: A solution is a homogeneous mixture with uniform composition throughout.
rubric.description: States that a solution is homogeneous.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying a solution as homogeneous or uniform throughout.

rubric.why: A solution consists of a solute dissolved in a solvent.
rubric.description: Names the components of a solution.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming both the solute and the solvent.

rubric.why: Solution particles are extremely small and cannot be seen individually.
rubric.description: Describes the size or visibility of solution particles.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the particles are very small or cannot be seen individually.

accept: cannot be separated by ordinary filtration
rubric.why: Solution particles remain dispersed and pass through ordinary filter paper.
rubric.description: States a characteristic of solution stability or filtration.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that particles do not settle or cannot be separated by ordinary filtration.

modelAnswer: A solution is a homogeneous mixture with uniform composition throughout.
It consists of a solute dissolved in a solvent.
Its particles are extremely small and cannot be seen individually.
The particles do not settle and cannot be separated by ordinary filtration.
